steps.title: What electrolysis is
steps.body:
**Electrolysis** uses electricity to break down an ionic compound into its elements. The compound being split is the **electrolyte**, and the current enters and leaves it through two **electrodes**, usually made of **graphite**, which conducts but does not react (it is *inert*).

The electrode connected to the **negative** terminal is the **cathode**; the one connected to the **positive** terminal is the **anode**.

It only works if the ions can **move**. In a solid the ions are locked in the lattice, so the compound must be **molten** (melted) or **dissolved** in water. Once free, the positive ions drift to the negative cathode and the negative ions drift to the positive anode: opposite charges attract.

visuals.alt: An electrolysis cell: a beaker of molten lead bromide with two graphite electrodes connected to a d.c. supply; lead ions move to the cathode and bromide ions to the anode, giving lead at the cathode and bromine at the anode

check.prompt: Which electrode is connected to the negative terminal of the supply?
check.solution: The **cathode** is negative; the **anode** is positive.
options: the cathode
the anode
both of them
neither; the electrolyte carries the negative charge

steps.title: Which ion goes where, and what forms
steps.body:
Ions are named by charge: positive ions are **cations** and go to the **cathode**; negative ions are **anions** and go to the **anode**. The names match, which is how to remember them.

At the electrodes the ions become atoms again:

- At the **cathode**, positive metal ions **gain electrons** from the electrode and become metal atoms. Molten lead bromide gives **lead**.
- At the **anode**, negative non-metal ions **lose electrons** to the electrode and become non-metal atoms, which pair up into molecules. Lead bromide gives **bromine**.

So a molten binary compound always splits into the **metal at the cathode** and the **non-metal at the anode**: sodium chloride gives sodium and chlorine; zinc chloride gives zinc and chlorine.

check.prompt: Molten sodium chloride is electrolysed. What forms at the cathode?
check.solution: **Sodium**: Na⁺ ions gain electrons at the cathode.

steps.title: How the current flows
steps.body:
A common misunderstanding: electrons do not swim through the electrolyte.

In the **wires**, the current is a flow of **electrons**, from the anode round the external circuit to the cathode. In the **electrolyte**, there are no free electrons: the current is carried by the **ions moving**, cations one way and anions the other.

At the surfaces of the electrodes the two kinds of current meet. Electrons arriving at the cathode are handed to cations; electrons are taken from anions at the anode and sent off round the wire. That hand-over is the chemistry.

This is also why a molten ionic compound conducts but a solid one does not, which you met in bonding: conduction needs charged particles that are free to move.

rows: cations to cathode, anions to anode
electrons handed to or taken from ions

check.prompt: What carries the current through a molten electrolyte?
check.solution: **Ions**. Electrons carry the current in the wires only.

moving atoms

steps.title: Extracting aluminium
steps.body:
Metals **more reactive than carbon** — aluminium, and everything above it in the reactivity series — cannot be extracted by heating their oxides with carbon, so they are extracted by **electrolysis**.

Aluminium comes from **bauxite**, which is purified to **aluminium oxide**, Al₂O₃. Its melting point is over 2000 °C, far too high to be practical, so it is **dissolved in molten cryolite**, which brings the working temperature down to around 950 °C and saves a great deal of energy.

The cell has **carbon electrodes**. At the cathode, aluminium forms and collects as a liquid. At the anode, **oxygen** forms — and at that temperature the oxygen **reacts with the carbon anode** to make carbon dioxide, so the anodes slowly burn away and have to be **replaced**.

The process is **expensive**: it uses a lot of electrical energy, and the anodes are a running cost. That is why recycling aluminium is worthwhile.

props.electrolyte: aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite

visuals.alt: The aluminium extraction cell: aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite with carbon electrodes; aluminium ions move to the cathode and oxide ions to the anode, giving aluminium and oxygen, and the oxygen burns the carbon anode to carbon dioxide

check.prompt: Why does the oxygen at the anode cause a problem?
check.solution: The hot carbon anode reacts with the oxygen to form **carbon dioxide**, so the anode is gradually used up and must be replaced.
options: It reacts with the carbon anode, which burns away as CO₂
It dissolves in the aluminium and weakens it
It puts out the heating flame under the cell
It turns the cryolite back into a solid

steps.title: Half equations: what happens at each electrode
steps.body: A **half equation** shows the reaction at one electrode, with the electrons written in. Two rules: at the cathode, ions **gain** electrons (electrons on the left); at the anode, ions **lose** electrons (electrons on the right). Balance the atoms, then balance the charge with the electrons.

steps.text: Pb²⁺ ions arrive at the cathode
Each needs 2 electrons to become neutral: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb
Charge check: 2+ and 2− on the left is 0; Pb on the right is 0 ✓
Br⁻ ions arrive at the anode
Bromine exists as Br₂, so two ions are needed: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻
Charge check: 2− on the left; Br₂ is 0 and 2e⁻ is 2− on the right ✓
steps.note: the electrons carry the charge across
two ions, four electrons, one O₂

check.prompt: Complete the anode half equation for molten sodium chloride: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + ?
check.solution: **2e⁻**: two chloride ions each lose one electron, so two electrons appear on the right.

steps.title: Oxidation and reduction: OIL RIG
steps.body:
You met oxidation as *gaining oxygen* in Year 9. The Higher-tier definition is in terms of **electrons**:

- **Oxidation Is Loss** of electrons.
- **Reduction Is Gain** of electrons.

**OIL RIG.** Now look at the electrodes again.

At the **cathode**, Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb: the ion **gains** electrons, so it is **reduced**. Reduction happens at the cathode.

At the **anode**, 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻: the ions **lose** electrons, so they are **oxidised**. Oxidation happens at the anode.

Both always happen together — the electrons lost at one electrode are the electrons gained at the other — which is why the whole process is called a **redox** reaction.

visuals.alt: A table matching each electrode to the direction of electron transfer and the redox word

check.prompt: In Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al, the aluminium ion is…
check.solution: Electrons on the left are **gained**; gain is **reduction** (RIG).
options: reduced, because it gains electrons
oxidised, because it gains electrons
reduced, because it loses electrons
oxidised, because it loses electrons

steps.title: Grade 9: balance the charge, explain the costs, and use the right words
steps.body:
**Balance charge as well as atoms.** 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ needs *four* electrons, because two ions each carry 2−. Count the charge on each side and make it equal; the electrons are what make it equal.

**Say why molten, in words the examiner wants.** *The ions are free to move and carry the current* — not *so it conducts*.

**The aluminium question has a shape.** Dissolve in cryolite (why: lower melting point, less energy) → electrolyse → aluminium at the cathode by reduction → oxygen at the anode by oxidation → oxygen burns the carbon anodes → replace anodes. Then the costs: electricity, and anodes. A six-mark answer wants all of it, in order.

**Reactivity decides the method.** Carbon can only reduce oxides of metals below it in the reactivity series; above carbon, electrolysis. Tie the choice to reactivity every time.

**Electrons and ions are different currents.** Electrons in the wires; ions in the electrolyte.

rows: molten, so the ions are free to move and carry the current
cryolite lowers the melting point, so less energy is needed
aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce its oxide; electrolysis is used
ions carry the current in the electrolyte; electrons in the wires

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Electrolysis** splits an ionic compound using electricity. **Electrolyte**: the compound; **electrodes**: cathode (−) and anode (+), usually graphite.
- The compound must be **molten or dissolved** so the **ions are free to move** and carry the current. In the wires, electrons carry it.
- **Cations → cathode**, gain electrons, form the **metal**. **Anions → anode**, lose electrons, form the **non-metal**.
- **Half equations**: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb; 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻; Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al; 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻. Balance atoms, then charge.
- **OIL RIG**: reduction at the cathode, oxidation at the anode.
- **Aluminium**: Al₂O₃ dissolved in **molten cryolite** (lower melting point), carbon electrodes; the anodes burn to CO₂ and are replaced; expensive because of the electricity and the anodes.
- Metals **more reactive than carbon** are extracted by electrolysis.

questions.prompt: Why can a solid ionic compound not be electrolysed?
questions.solution: In a solid the ions are held in the lattice; electrolysis needs **ions that can move** to the electrodes, so the compound must be **molten** or dissolved.

markScheme.description: ions cannot move in a solid

options: Its ions are fixed in place and cannot move
It has no ions at all
It does not contain any electrons
It is not a good insulator

questions.prompt: What is the name of the negative electrode?
questions.solution: The **cathode** is the negative electrode. It attracts positive ions (cations).

questions.prompt: Molten lead bromide is electrolysed. Name the product at the anode.
questions.solution: **Bromine.** Bromide ions, Br⁻, are negative, so they move to the positive anode, lose electrons and form bromine.

questions.prompt: What is the electrolyte in the extraction of aluminium?
questions.solution: Purified **aluminium oxide** is dissolved in **molten cryolite**. Water cannot be used: aluminium is more reactive than hydrogen, so an aqueous solution would give hydrogen instead.
options: Aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite
Aluminium chloride dissolved in water
Molten aluminium metal
Bauxite dissolved in dilute acid

questions.prompt: Which ion moves to the cathode when molten sodium chloride is electrolysed?
questions.solution: The **sodium ion, Na⁺**. Positive ions move to the negative cathode, where each gains an electron to form sodium metal.

questions.prompt: Why is cryolite used in the extraction of aluminium?
questions.solution: Aluminium oxide melts above 2000 °C. Dissolving it in molten **cryolite** lets the cell run at a much lower temperature, so less energy is used and the process is cheaper.

markScheme.description: lowers the melting point, saves energy

options: It lowers the melting point of the mixture, saving energy
It reacts with the aluminium oxide to release aluminium
It stops the aluminium from oxidising in the air
It conducts electricity when the oxide cannot

questions.prompt: Explain why the positive electrodes in an aluminium electrolysis cell have to be replaced regularly.
questions.solution: A chain: oxygen is produced at the anode; the anode is made of carbon; at the high temperature the carbon reacts with the oxygen to form carbon dioxide, so the anode burns away.

markScheme.description: oxygen is produced at the positive electrode
the electrode is carbon (graphite), which reacts with the oxygen
forming carbon dioxide, so the electrode wears away

criteria.text: Oxygen forms at the positive electrode
The carbon electrode reacts with the oxygen at the high temperature
Carbon dioxide forms and the electrode burns away, so it must be replaced

questions.modelAnswer: Oxygen is produced at the positive electrode. The electrodes are made of carbon, and at the high temperature of the cell the carbon reacts with the oxygen to form carbon dioxide. The electrode is gradually burnt away, so it has to be replaced.

questions.prompt: Which metal is extracted by electrolysis rather than by reduction with carbon?
questions.solution: **Aluminium** is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot take the oxygen from its oxide. Iron, zinc and copper are less reactive than carbon and are extracted by heating their oxides with carbon.
options: aluminium
iron
copper
zinc

questions.prompt: Complete the half equation for the cathode in the electrolysis of molten lead bromide: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → ?
questions.solution: **Pb.** Each lead ion gains two electrons and becomes a lead atom: *Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb*. Gaining electrons is **reduction**.

questions.prompt: At which electrode does oxidation happen, and why?
questions.solution: **OIL RIG**: oxidation is loss of electrons. Negative ions give up electrons at the **anode**, so oxidation happens there; positive ions gain electrons at the cathode, which is reduction.
options: The anode, because ions lose electrons there
The cathode, because ions lose electrons there
The anode, because ions gain electrons there
The cathode, because ions gain electrons there

questions.prompt: Write the half equation for the reaction at the anode when molten sodium chloride is electrolysed.
questions.solution: *2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻*. Two chloride ions each lose one electron and join to make a chlorine molecule. Check it balances: two chlorines each side, and the charge is 2− on the left and 2− on the right (the two electrons).

markScheme.description: Cl⁻ losing electrons to form Cl₂

questions.prompt: Write the half equation for the reaction at the cathode in the extraction of aluminium.
questions.solution: *Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al*. Each aluminium ion needs three electrons to become an atom, one for each positive charge.

questions.prompt: In the half equation 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻, which statement is correct?
questions.solution: Oxide ions **lose** electrons (four between two of them), and loss of electrons is **oxidation**. This happens at the anode.
options: The oxide ions are oxidised, because they lose electrons
The oxide ions are reduced, because they lose electrons
The oxide ions are oxidised, because they gain electrons
Oxygen is reduced, because it gains electrons

questions.prompt: Describe how aluminium is extracted from aluminium oxide, and explain why the process is expensive.
questions.solution: Method, then costs. Aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite; the mixture is electrolysed with carbon electrodes; Al³⁺ ions gain electrons at the cathode to form aluminium (Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al); oxide ions lose electrons at the anode to form oxygen (2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻); the oxygen reacts with the carbon anodes, which burn away as CO₂. Expensive because: large amounts of electricity are needed to melt the mixture and to keep the current flowing, and the anodes have to be replaced regularly.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): some relevant points, such as electrolysis is used, or it needs a lot of electricity
Level 2 (3 to 4): the process described with cryolite and the products at each electrode, and one cost reason
Level 3 (5 to 6): both half equations or the electrode reactions explained as electron transfer, the anode reaction with oxygen, and both cost reasons

criteria.text: Aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite, then electrolysed
Aluminium at the cathode: Al³⁺ gains electrons (reduction)
Oxygen at the anode: O²⁻ loses electrons (oxidation)
Carbon anodes react with the oxygen to form CO₂ and are replaced
Costs: large amounts of electrical energy
Costs: cryolite and the replacement of the anodes, or the energy to melt

questions.modelAnswer: Aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite, which lowers the melting point, and the mixture is electrolysed using carbon electrodes. At the cathode, aluminium ions gain electrons and are reduced to aluminium: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al. At the anode, oxide ions lose electrons and are oxidised to oxygen: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻. The oxygen reacts with the hot carbon anodes to form carbon dioxide, so the anodes burn away and must be replaced. The process is expensive because a large amount of electrical energy is needed to melt the electrolyte and drive the electrolysis, and because the anodes have to be replaced regularly.

questions.prompt: Molten zinc chloride is electrolysed. Which pair gives the product at each electrode?
questions.skill: predicting products of a molten compound
questions.solution: A molten binary compound gives the **metal at the cathode** and the **non-metal at the anode**: zinc and chlorine. Hydrogen and oxygen only appear when water is present.

markScheme.description: zinc at the cathode, chlorine at the anode

options: cathode: zinc · anode: chlorine
cathode: chlorine · anode: zinc
cathode: hydrogen · anode: chlorine
cathode: zinc · anode: oxygen

questions.prompt: Write the half equation for the anode reaction in the electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide.
questions.solution: *2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻*. Two oxide ions, each with a 2− charge, lose four electrons in total to form one oxygen molecule. Charge check: 4− on the left, 4− on the right.

markScheme.description: O²⁻ losing electrons to form O₂

questions.prompt: A student says electrons flow through the molten electrolyte from the anode to the cathode. What is wrong?
questions.solution: In the external circuit the current is electrons in the wires. Inside the electrolyte there are no free electrons: the current is carried by **ions moving** to the electrodes. That is why the compound has to be molten.

markScheme.description: ions carry the current in the electrolyte

options: Electrons flow through the wires; in the electrolyte the current is carried by moving ions
Electrons flow from the cathode to the anode through the electrolyte
Nothing: electrons carry the current everywhere in the circuit
Electrons do not move at all during electrolysis

questions.prompt: Explain, in terms of electrons, why the reaction at the cathode is a reduction and the reaction at the anode is an oxidation, using molten lead bromide as the example.
questions.solution: Cathode: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb, the lead ion gains electrons, and gain of electrons is reduction. Anode: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻, bromide ions lose electrons, and loss of electrons is oxidation. The electrons lost at the anode travel round the external circuit to the cathode.
questions.modelAnswer: At the cathode, lead ions gain two electrons each: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb. Gaining electrons is reduction, so the lead ions are reduced. At the anode, bromide ions each lose an electron and pair up: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻. Losing electrons is oxidation, so the bromide ions are oxidised. The electrons released at the anode flow through the external circuit to the cathode.

examTechnique.body:
Electrolysis is on Paper 1 and is asked in three ways: predict the products, write half equations, and explain the extraction of aluminium. Predicting products from a molten compound is mechanical — metal at the cathode, non-metal at the anode — as long as you say which electrode is which. Half equations are Higher tier and are marked on balance: atoms first, then charge, with the electrons doing the balancing.

The aluminium question is a six-marker with a fixed shape: cryolite and why, the electrode reactions as electron transfer, the anodes burning away, and the costs. Use the words the mark scheme uses: ions free to move, gain and loss of electrons, reduction and oxidation, and reactivity compared with carbon.
examinerErrors: Saying a solid conducts once it is *heated* rather than *molten*: the ions must be free to move.
Swapping the electrodes: the cathode is negative and attracts positive ions.
Half equations with the right atoms but unbalanced charge, such as O²⁻ → O₂ + 2e⁻.
Writing that cryolite reacts with the aluminium oxide; it only lowers the melting point.
Explaining the anode wearing away without naming the reaction: carbon reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide.
Saying electrons flow through the electrolyte.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer predicts the products of any molten compound and says which electrode gives which, writes half equations balanced for atoms and charge, and labels each as oxidation or reduction in terms of electrons. It explains the aluminium cell in full, from cryolite to replaced anodes, links the choice of electrolysis to reactivity relative to carbon, and keeps electrons in the wires and ions in the electrolyte.
